input.question: How closely and with how much detail could astronomers see Jupiter in the 17th century?
input.ground_truth: Obviously this was before photography was invented, but many of these early telescopic astronomers did leave us drawings of their views of Jupiter: - Galileo Galilei left [these drawing from 1610 detailing the positions of Jupiter's moons](_URL_0_). Not much is seen of Jupiter itself other than a disc. - Robert Hooke, generally credited with discovering the Great Red Spot, had a better telescope and made [this drawing of Jupiter in 1666](_URL_2_). - Giovanni Cassini had a considerably better telescope than either. [Here are some of his drawings from 1665, 1672, and 1677.](_URL_1_)

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big, round ball (that’s Jupiter) really, really far away. In the 1600s, people didn’t have telescopes like we do now—they had simple ones that just made things a little bigger and clearer.

So, if you looked at Jupiter with a 17th-century telescope, you could see that it’s a round ball, not a star. You might even see that it looks a little bit fuzzy, not just like a tiny dot. Some very smart people, like Galileo, saw that Jupiter has some little dots next to it! Those were Jupiter’s four biggest moons.

But you couldn’t see all the pretty stripes and the big red spot on Jupiter like we can today. It would just look like a fuzzy, round ball with some tiny spots next to it. Not as clear or colorful as a picture from a modern telescope!
